title: Autonomous BTSbot-nearby follow-up captures an infant supernova’s flash spectrum and constrains progenitor mass loss
summary: The BTSbot-nearby system used the BTSbot machine-learning classifier to identify SN 2024jlf in ZTF data and autonomously trigger a spectroscopic follow-up request, enabling spectroscopy about 0.7 days after first light. The early spectra showed short-lived Hα, He II and C IV flash-ionization features; comparison with two radiative-hydrodynamics model grids constrained the red-supergiant progenitor’s enhanced pre-explosion mass-loss rate to roughly 10⁻⁴–10⁻³ solar masses per year.
ai_technology: BTSbot machine-learning transient classifier integrated with the BTSbot-nearby autonomous follow-up program
organization: Northwestern University; California Institute of Technology; Stockholm University; Liverpool John Moores University; NSF-Simons AI Institute for the Sky; Zwicky Transient Facility collaboration

evidence.tested: The BTSbot-nearby system used the BTSbot machine-learning classifier to identify SN 2024jlf in ZTF data and autonomously trigger a spectroscopic follow-up request, enabling spectroscopy about 0.7 days after first light.
evidence.unknown: The AI contribution is event identification and automated prioritization, not inference of the stellar mass-loss physics. The rate is model-dependent and derived from two radiative-hydrodynamics code grids under adopted wind assumptions. The paper reports an individual nearby Type IIP event; this is not a population-level claim. The transient was originally reported to the Transient Name Server by a human observer, while the BTSbot-nearby program supplied rapid automated follow-up.
evidence.ai_role: BTSbot identified the transient in ZTF alert data; host-distance and youth filters in BTSbot-nearby automatically triggered target-of-opportunity spectroscopy. This shortened latency to approximately seven minutes from alert-filter pass to first spectrum (spectroscopy was obtained about 0.7 days after first light), enabling observation of ephemeral flash features. Human and instrument teams obtained/interpreted observations; radiation-hydrodynamics models supported the mass-loss inference.
